title: Precisely how long is a 'moment'? | TIME WORDS

entries.note: Means a span or period, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to divide; it replaced Old English [[see:tide]], and contrasts with Latin [[see:tempus]], meaning to stretch.
The Old English word for time before 'time'; it referred to the sea's movement and was also used for an hour before [[see:hour]] was borrowed from French.
The Latin word for time, which the hosts say comes from the idea of stretching, unlike the Germanic sense of dividing behind [[see:time]].
Imitates the sound of an early square sheet-metal bell; adopted in the 14th century probably from medieval Latin, possibly borrowed earlier from Celtic; compare German [[same-root:Glocke]].
The German word the hosts link to [[same-root:clock]], familiar from the glockenspiel and sounding much like it.
An Old English word for a timepiece, used before [[see:clock]] arrived in the 14th century.
The Latin word for a timepiece, which gave [[gave:horology]].
Comes from [[from:horologium]]; it keeps the H that [[see:hour]] does not pronounce, and timepieces are still called horological.
The Greek water clock, which 'stole' water from one bowl into another so the amount fallen measured time; related to [[same-root:kleptomaniac]].
Shares the 'thief' element of [[same-root:κλεψύδρα]], the Greek water clock.
The French word for a clock, contrasted with English keeping the Germanic-sounding [[see:clock]].
A sophisticated water-powered astronomical clock from the Islamic Golden Age, called the earliest programmable analogue computer.
Named for our looking at it, while other languages name it for showing the time, like French [[equivalent:montre]].
The French word for a [[equivalent:watch]], named for showing the time.
The German word for a [[equivalent:watch]], which simply means a clock or a time.
Means the thing opposite or facing you, which is why a watch or clock has a face.
The unit of time and the ordinal are one word, from Latin [[from:secunda minuta]]; the ordinal came with the Normans and replaced [[see:other]].
The small parts of an hour divided a second time, which gave [[gave:second]].
Same word as minute meaning tiny: a small part of an hour, from [[from:pars minuta prima]]; the original minute was a tenth of an hour.
The first small part of an hour, which gave [[gave:minute]]; dividing it again gave [[see:secunda minuta]].
Used in English for the thing after first until the Normans brought [[see:second]].
Goes back to Greek [[from:ὥρα]]; its H has never been pronounced in English, French or Spanish [[see:hora]], although it is still written.
The Spanish word for [[equivalent:hour]], whose H has never been pronounced.
Greek for a unit of the day, a season or any interval, which gave [[gave:hour]]; it shares an ancient root with [[same-root:year]].
A very old native word going back to Proto-Indo-European, probably related to [[same-root?:ὥρα]]; its root means both year and season.
A very old word from a Proto-Germanic root meaning to burn or be hot; it first meant the daylight period in contrast to night. Related to Sanskrit [[same-root:dāha]].
Sanskrit for a glow, specifically a glowing in the sky, which the hosts say is clearly related to [[same-root:day]].
Discussed in a past episode: time zones were 'wibbly wobbly' until railways needed standard time so engines wouldn't collide at stations.
The 8th-century Venerable Bede described the Anglo-Saxon system dividing an hour into [[see:point]]s, [[see:moment]]s, [[see:ounce]]s and [[see:atom]]s.
A medieval unit of time: a quarter of an hour, made of ten [[see:moment]]s, as described by Bartholomeus Anglicus; also called a [[see:prick]].
A medieval unit of time: a tenth of a [[see:point]], made up of twelve [[see:ounce]]s.
A medieval unit of time: a twelfth of a [[see:moment]], made up of 47 [[see:atom]]s.
The smallest medieval unit of time, meaning indivisible: 47 to an [[see:ounce]], 22,560 to an hour, far too small to have been measured.
Jess asks whether the medieval [[unrelated:atom]] of time relates to the atomic clock; Rob says it doesn't.
Another word for the medieval [[equivalent:point]] of time, which Rob finds juvenilely funny; pun-fodder throughout English literature.
The darkest part of the day that isn't night, the same word as [[same-root:dusky]]; Old English dox underwent metathesis, like [[see:ask]].
Means somewhat dark; the same word as [[same-root:dusk]].
Ask and its form axe are given as an example of metathesis, like that in [[see:dusk]].
From Latin nona, the ninth hour counting from 6 a.m., so originally about 3 p.m. before moving to midday; gave [[gave:afternoon]] and [[gave:forenoon]].
Began as references to 'after noon' and became one word; from [[from:noon]].
Once used for the morning, from 'before noon'; from [[from:noon]], now rarely used.
The light between, when the sun is below the horizon; originally it referred to both morning and evening.
From the Latin for twilight or dusk; describes twilight hours and species active at [[see:twilight]].
Coined by Shakespeare, who clipped the -ing from the earlier word [[from:dawning]]; also covered in their Shakespeare episode.
Swahili time starts the day at 6 a.m., since its speakers live near the equator, so 7:00 is one o'clock; clocks put six at the top.
The Babylonians divided daylight into twelve parts, so hours were longer in summer and shorter in winter.
Romans used twelve daylight hours recalculated daily, so water clocks and sundials needed constant seasonal adjustment.
Medieval monasteries marked hours with bells and prayers, not clocks, which may explain why [[see:noon]] was named at all.
A dechristianised calendar with twelve 30-day months, each split into three ten-day weeks called a [[see:décade]], alongside [[see:decimal hour]]s.
The ten-day week of the [[see:French Revolutionary calendar]], meaning ten days rather than ten years.
France decimalised time from 1794 to 1800: ten decimal hours a day, each of 100 decimal minutes of 100 decimal seconds.
The base-12 system, discussed in their numbers and mathematics episode.
Mentioned by Rob alongside [[see:duodecimal]] as discussed in their numbers and mathematics episode.
German for 12:30, half an hour before one, which trips up English speakers for whom [[see:half one]] means 1:30.
British English for 1:30, which clashes with German [[see:halb eins]], meaning 12:30; some find this English phrasing uncouth.
What Germans would say for 1:30, though Rob finds people often just say 1:30 to him; compare [[see:half one]].
The American phrasing Jess finds clearer than British [[see:half one]].
A Scottish friend's way of saying 6:30 that confused Jess's group in Cannes; compare [[see:half one]].
A joke in the Philippines that Filipino time means being late; compare [[equivalent:Indian Standard Time]].
Jess's Indian friends joke that it means turning up an hour late, like [[equivalent:Filipino time]].
Meant a turning or succession, sharing a root with [[same-root:vice versa]] and [[same-root:vicarious]]; one theory links it to a change of duty, like [[see:vika]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with [[same-root:week]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with [[same-root:week]].
Old Icelandic for a distance travelled at sea, possibly before changing rowers, supporting the change-of-duty theory of [[same-root:week]].
Moon day, named after the moon, which also gives us [[see:month]]; the days are covered in their mythology episode.
Named after [[from:Tiw]], the Germanic god of war.
Odin's day, from the Germanic translation of Roman planetary day names; the god was [[from:Woden]] to the Anglo-Saxons.
Thor's day, one of the Germanic translations of Roman day names after deities.
Generally thought to be named after [[from:Frigg]] rather than the similar [[see:Freya]].
Back to Latin: named after Saturn.
Named after the sun.
The Germanic god of war after whom [[see:Tuesday]] is named.
The Anglo-Saxon name for Odin, behind [[see:Wednesday]].
The goddess generally thought to be behind [[see:Friday]]; similar to, but not the same as, [[see:Freya]].
Jess's first guess for the goddess behind [[see:Friday]]; Rob says it is generally thought to be the similar [[see:Frigg]].
From Latin calendarium, an account book or debt register, because interest was due on the [[from:kalends]].
The first day of the Roman month, from [[from:calare]], to call out, because priests publicly proclaimed it after seeing the new moon.
A Germanic word that shares a Proto-Indo-European root with Latin [[same-root:calare]], behind [[see:kalends]].
Literally the sun standing still; knowing the etymology helps Rob tell it apart from [[see:equinox]].
Literally equal night.
A period of two weeks, from Old English for fourteen nights; rare in the US; its counterpart was [[see:sennight]].
From seven nights, a now-unused word for a week; the counterpart of [[see:fortnight]].
Used since Old English for a period of twelve months, distinct from the calendar [[see:year]]; it appears in [[see:All Around My Hat]].
An 1800s folk song, sung by Rob, that uses [[see:twelvemonth]] in 'for a twelvemonth and a day'.
A lost word for the day before yesterday; compare German [[equivalent:vorgestern]].
A lost word for the day after tomorrow, like German [[equivalent:übermorgen]]; the hosts want to bring it back because it sounds modern and fun.
The German word for the day after tomorrow, still in use; the equivalent of [[equivalent:overmorrow]].
German for the day before yesterday; adding more vor- prefixes goes further back; the equivalent of [[equivalent:ereyesterday]].

Related to measurement and roughly a lunar cycle; linked to [[same-root:meter]], [[same-root:dimension]], [[same-root:menstrual]], [[same-root:menopause]], [[same-root:semester]] and [[same-root:trimester]].
Ultimately related to [[same-root:month]].
Ultimately related to [[same-root:month]].
Related to [[same-root:month]].
Related to [[same-root:month]].
Means three months, not a division into three, which Rob realised during his wife's pregnancy.
From the Latin for six months, not a half, though semesters rarely last six months now; like [[see:trimester]].
Also called the Platonic year: about 25,920 years (now 25,800) for Earth's slowly drifting axis to return to its original position.
Earth's axis points at it only temporarily; it won't again for over 25,000 years, because of the [[see:great year]] cycle.
Essentially means a sowing; used more generally until the 14th century, when four fixed seasons were settled on.
Means to winterise yourself, evoking the French name for winter.
The US name for the season, suggesting decay and dying; like [[see:autumn]], unusual among Germanic languages, which mostly called it [[see:harvest]].
The British name, taken from French and said to mean increase; neither it nor [[see:fall]] was the original English term, [[see:harvest]].
What English called the season before [[see:fall]] and [[see:autumn]], as many other Germanic languages still do.
One of the scarier Anglo-Saxon month names, discussed in their calendar episode, all of which ended in 'monath'.
The Anglo-Saxon month when cows were milked extra; covered in their calendar episode with the other month names.
